planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; introduced in 1845 and named for Lancashire weaver-botanist John Horsefield, Horsfieldii was one of the first bicolor trumpet daffodils raised.

directions: Plant bulbs 5-6 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade in fall. Horsfieldii, introduced in 1845 and named for Lancashire weaver and amateur botanist John Horsefield, was one of the earliest bicolor trumpet hybrids to reach commerce, pairing a broad snow-white perianth with a strong, flaring yellow trumpet, a combination novel enough in its day to influence generations of later bicolor breeding. The sturdy, early-to-midseason blooms hold up well to spring wind and rain. Let foliage ripen naturally after flowering and leave established clumps undisturbed for several years before dividing.

common_name: Mary Copeland Daffodil (Historic Double White-and-Orange Daffodil)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; named and introduced in 1913 by breeder W.F.M. Copeland for his daughter, with creamy white outer petals and a center flecked orange and pale yellow.

directions: Plant bulbs 5-6 inches deep in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to light shade in fall. Mary Copeland produces fully double, mid-season flowers in which the creamy outer petals surround a tightly packed center mottled with orange and soft yellow segments, a color combination distinctive among doubles of its era. Named by breeder W.F.M. Copeland for his young daughter and introduced in 1913, it has persisted in heirloom bulb collections for over a century. Deadhead spent blooms if desired but let the foliage die back fully before cutting it, and give the clump a top-dress of compost in fall to sustain repeat flowering.

common_name: Sulphur Phoenix Daffodil (Antique Pale Double Narcissus, Codlins and Cream)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; one of the old double daffodils long known in English gardens as Codlins and Cream, also traded as Silver Phoenix.

directions: Plant bulbs 5-6 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade in fall. Sulphur Phoenix carries loosely doubled, pale creamy-sulphur flowers with occasional pale orange flecks near the center, a soft antique coloring quite different from the brighter doubles bred in more recent decades. It is one of the old double narcissus long known in English cottage gardens as Codlins and Cream, also traded under the name Silver Phoenix, and documented in commerce by the early twentieth century. Leave foliage to ripen fully after bloom and avoid disturbing established clumps, since this heirloom can be slow to settle in after replanting.

common_name: Orange Phoenix Daffodil (Antique White-and-Orange Double Narcissus, Eggs and Bacon)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; a sibling 'Phoenix' double, closely related to Sulphur Phoenix, long grown under the old cottage-garden name Eggs and Bacon.

directions: Plant bulbs 5-6 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade in fall. Orange Phoenix bears shaggy double white flowers heavily flecked with orange and scarlet through the center, a bolder companion to the paler Sulphur Phoenix and one of the oldest doubles still traded under its original name, long known in English gardens as Eggs and Bacon. Its irregular, informal form and heirloom pedigree have kept it in demand among collectors of antique bulbs despite being largely eclipsed commercially by modern doubles. Let the foliage yellow and collapse naturally before removing it, and expect this old variety to take a season or two to settle before flowering freely.

common_name: Double Roman Daffodil (Ancient Fragrant Double Tazetta)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade in mild climates, or pot for indoor forcing in cold climates; Double Roman is an old, Mediterranean-rooted tazetta prized for its intense fragrance and reliability as a forcing bulb.

directions: In mild climates, plant bulbs 4-5 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade in fall; in colder regions grow it as a forced indoor bulb in bowls of gravel or soil, starting six to eight weeks before desired bloom. Double Roman produces clusters of intensely fragrant, creamy-white double flowers brushed with soft orange-yellow at the center, an old tazetta form grown in Mediterranean and European gardens for generations before it was carried into American gardens as a treasured pass-along bulb. Unlike hardy trumpet types it does not require a hard winter chill to flower, which is what makes it such a dependable choice for forcing and for warm-winter Southern gardens alike. Keep forced bulbs cool and bright to prevent weak, floppy stems.

common_name: Queen of Spain Daffodil (Historic Pale Yellow Nodding Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained, gritty soil in full sun to light shade; Queen of Spain is an old hybrid daffodil with slender, nodding, pale primrose-yellow flowers and a graceful, elongated trumpet.

directions: Plant bulbs 4-5 inches deep in gritty, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade in fall, ideally in a rock garden or raised bed where drainage is sharp. Queen of Spain carries slender, nodding, pale primrose flowers with a long, gracefully flared trumpet and swept-back petals, a refined look that made it a favorite among Victorian-era collectors of species-type hybrids. It is smaller and more delicate than modern trumpet daffodils and resents heavy, wet soil, so avoid sites that stay soggy over winter. Leave the fine foliage undisturbed until it yellows, since this slow-multiplying heirloom rebuilds its bulb more gradually than vigorous modern cultivars.
